children: Webhook listeners — like any other piece of software — will eventually become unstable or unavailable due to network or system issues. Some webhook providers — such as
and provide resiliency features to reduce the burden on webhook consumers. Examples of interesting features include:

children.name: p
children: : Webhook providers regularly reach out to webhook listeners to check their status. If a listener is unavailable, the provider takes action — such as queueing notifications or sending alerts to system admins — until the webhook listener gets fixed. This feature is helpful, especially in webhooks that don't send messages often.
, for example, sends a heartbeat with an empty
array every eight hours and deletes webhooks that go 24 hours without a successful response.

children.name: Fence
p
children: : webhook providers can keep track of historical information of webhook events sent and allow consumers to send messages again after failures or unavailability. Queues can be implemented on listener errors or in conjunction with heartbeat checks. See
for how long major providers keep retrying.

children.name: p
children: : Some webhook providers implement circuit breaking logic to throttle and alleviate requests to webhook listeners when webhook requests cross an error or response time threshold.
temporarily disables a webhook after four consecutive failures — for one minute at first, growing to 24 hours — and permanently after 40.
delays notifications for 10 minutes when more than 10% of responses take longer than 3 seconds.

frontmatter.title: Heartbeat, Queueing, and Circuit Breaking
frontmatter.description: Webhook listeners — like any other piece of software — will eventually become unstable or unavailable due to network or system issues. Good webhook providers recognize availability as an inevitable problem and provide resiliency features to reduce the burden on webhook consumers.
